course_title: Theory and Society in the Pacific
course_description:
This course introduces anthropological and other theoretical perspectives on and from the societies, scholars and peoples of the Pacific - from American Samoa and Hawai'i to the Marshall Islands, Papua New Guinea and West Papua. It is not a traditional review of the history of anthropological thought, but rather, in this course, `theory' means diverse interpretations and understandings of society. Through an exploration of racism/colonialism, culture and gender it prepares students to engage more deeply with challenges such as climate change, gender equality, and decolonisation and provides a grounding in Pacific anthropology.

This course is essential preparation for graduates to obtain a foundational understanding of contemporary conditions, debates, and analyses in the Pacific region so you can engage ethically and respectfully in the region or with Pasifika peoples around the world. The 'learning resources' list contains course readings.

course_aims: The aims of this course are:

learning_outcomes.description: Identify, evaluate and challenge how anthropology engages with Pacific societies, peoples, and cultures.
Demonstrate an awareness of Pasifika/Pacific perspectives that challenge historical biases and can be applied to engage ethically and respectfully with Pasifika peoples.
Demonstrate competence with contemporary anthropological concepts and scholarship in relation to key issues in the Pacific/Oceania region.

assessment_details.task_description: Students will visit the museum during class time (visit approx 60 minutes) and then return to the classroom to write an object-based critical research proposal (500 words max, approx 60 minutes). The proposal will -- a. Describe the object you chose while undertaking the museum visit. b. Using one area of debate or key concept from lectures and readings in week 1, 2 & 4 (e.g., mobility, personhood, commodity, value), explain a research question that might drive a research project about the museum object and its related peoples. Students will write their responses by hand or by electronic submission (Inspera). Students will have access to 1 page (double sided) hard copy and/or offline notes, plus downloaded/printed copies of relevant readings from week 1, 2 & 4. If students are absent due to illness, or other legitimate reason, an alternate time for writing will be scheduled. Marking criteria: Criteria including rubrics are available in the ‘Assessments’ folder on the course Blackboard site. AI Use: This assessment task will be completed in-person. assessment_details.title: Topic and reading reflections
assessment_details.other_conditions: Time limited, Secure. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: You will write two (2) reflections on the content of guest lecture modules (20% each) - 500 words max each, in class (60 mins) reflection week 6&7 Guest Dr Inez Fainga'a-Manu Sione - Pacific Communities and Cultures - completed in week 7 reflection week 8&9 Guest Prof Kristen Lyons - Development and Climate Change - completed in week 9 Each reflection should be written in the first person (e.g. "While reading the work of Pacific scholar, Hau'ofa, I found the way he addressed the topic of..."), and include both clear knowledge of material at hand and personal learning process ("Reflecting on the questions of 'development', made me question... ). For each topic/reading reflection, students will be assessed on how they - demonstrate engagement with readings and lecture content for the relevant weeks (summary/ content knowledge) 10/20 demonstrate reflection on values, thoughts, feelings, and ideas on the topic at hand. For example, are your values or ideas shifting? Being challenged? What questions arise in ethical or political terms? assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
This assessment item must be submitted via Turnitin on Blackboard Ultra.
Refer to the eLearning Guides for steps on how to submit your Turnitin assignment. No emailed assessments will be accepted. Students must obtain a Digital Receipt as evidence of successful submission of their assessment.
Students must abide by the Student Code of Conduct Policy which outlines that all submitted assessment must be their own work, except where properly referenced.
If you are experiencing technical difficulties with Blackboard or Turnitin, please contact the ITS Support Team .
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 28 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
A request for an extension must be submitted as soon as it becomes evident that an extension is needed, and no later than the assessment due date and time. Please refer to the my.UQ Applying for an assessment extension page for information.
Extension requests are processed by the School of Social Science Administration Team. Course Coordinators are unable to grant extensions directly. Extensions in your final semester of study could delay your graduation to the next graduation period.
Late Extension Applications
Late applications must include supporting documentation outlining how it was impossible, or unsafe, for you to have applied by the due date and time. The School of Social Science will not accept personal statements.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
Assessments will not be accepted if it is more than one week (7 calendar days) late without prior approval.

learning_activities.topic: Worlds of theory and society. The Pacific : ideas, people, things and place Introduction to the course, expectations and discussion of reading material for the week. Students are expected to read the required reading material before the class, and to bring notes and questions associated with those materials to the seminar. Required and recommended readings for each week are available via the course list on the library website (search on "ANTH2020"). Please consult -- The library course readings page for weekly required reading Blackboard for the document "Activities and reading summary" available on blackboard for detail of required and recommended readings Blackboard, weekly activities for questions that will guide what to focus on in relation to required and recommended readings Required reading is Epeli Hau'ofa plus at least one other required reading, as listed. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

The current-contemporary Pacific: mobility, exchange, value Pacific scholars and anthropologists challenge ideas of place, belonging, identity and mobility - What do these concepts mean in the history of scholarship the Pacific and how do they characterise the Pacific as a particular place about which to think about society, culture and reality? We also examine and consider the history of concepts such as 'the gift', value, and commodity, and engage with material-focussed research questions. This class will contain detailed guidance to prepare students for the in-class assessment in Week 4 Required reading is Thomas (1991) plus at least one other of the listed articles. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Public holiday - no class Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Anthropology Museum and assessment Anthropology Museum : This class will involve participation in a Museum exercise (approx. 60mins) and then an in-class exam designed to be completed in 60 minutes. Student will have the entire class time to complete the assessment. To address the exam question, students should make use of reading and audiovisual material from this week (4) plus week 1 & 2. See assessment details. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Geopolitics, economics and race Notions and contestations of race have always been present in anthropological engagements with Pacific peoples, and vice versa. How does race inform colonialism, geopolitics and contemporary economic relations in the Pacific? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Pacific Communities in Australia Guest Lecture by Dr. Inez Fainga’a-Manu Sione will lead discussions on concepts such as Indigenous knowledge and methodologies; collective/individual; voice, community. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

When two worlds collide: Pacific Cultural Adoptions in Australia. Dr Inez Fainga’a-Manu Sione Will lead discussions on concepts of : Personhood, kinship, family. In the final 60 minutes of the seminar, students will write a reflection on learning materials (lecture content and literature) from this week and/or the previous. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Experiencing Environments: Climate Change and the Pacific Guest lecture, Professor Kristen Lyons Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Centring women and Indigenous pathways in Development: Conservation and Food justice Outcomes Guest lecture, Professor Kristen Lyons The final 30 minutes of this class, students will write and submit a written reflection. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Ethnographic film 1: History, theory, and practice This seminar will consider the genre of ethnographic film through the history of filmmaking and anthropology, the visual 'eye' of the lens for ethnography, particularly for Pacific peoples, and some of the ways that ethnographic film practice has changed more recently. There will be a short lecture followed by discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Ethnographic film 2. Film: An Extraordinary Wedding & discussion This class will involve watching the film "An Extraordinary Wedding" and discussing its content, ethics and aesthetics in the context of the history of ethnographic film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Ethnographic film 3. Film: On Behalf of the living & discussion This class will involve watching the film "On Behalf of the living" and discussing its content, politics and relational message in the context of the history of ethnographic film. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Course Conclusion We will recap core material and discuss final queries on submission of final essay. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
